events.text:
This is game 180 in a series of 9×9 Go games. Each new game starts in a fresh session.

## Your goal

To become as strong at Go as you can: to keep improving, game after game, toward grandmaster-level play. The concrete target is to win consistently against the strongest opponent on the ladder, the 9d profile.

## What carries over

This session starts with no memory of the earlier ones: your conversation is not carried over. Your working directory does carry over: every file in it stays as you leave it. If CLAUDE.md exists there, it is loaded into your context at the start of every session; your other files are there to read with the file tools. What a later session knows of your earlier games is what you have left in these files.

Your working directory holds:
- CLAUDE.md (252,844 bytes)
- after.py (1,325 bytes)
- b.txt (297 bytes)
- count.py (828 bytes)
- g.txt (297 bytes)
- libs.py (1,378 bytes)

## This game

A new game. You play White, so your opponent moves first, right after you choose it.

Rules: Chinese area scoring, with 7 points of komi for White; a level score is a draw. Simple ko: an immediate recapture is refused, and the board marks the ko point when there is one. Suicide is not allowed. An invalid move is refused with the rule it broke, and the turn stays with you. The game ends after two passes in a row or a resignation; a game that reaches 243 moves is scored where it stands. After two passes the engine scores the position as it stands and decides itself which stones are dead.

## Opponents

Your opponent is KataGo playing in the style of a human of the rank you choose. The ladder, weakest to strongest: 20k, 18k, 16k, 14k, 12k, 10k, 8k, 6k, 4k, 2k, 1d, 3d, 5d, 7d, 9d. You choose the rank with `choose_opponent(rank)` before the first move; it holds for the whole game, and you choose again in the next game.

## Tools

- Go: `choose_opponent(rank)`, `board()`, `play(move)` with a point or `pass`, and `resign()`.
- Files: your Read, Write, Edit, Glob and Grep tools, for any file in your working directory.

You also have a shell, and you may write and run code in it; Python is available as `python3`. Use it only to inspect the current position and keep records — for example, to count stones or liberties, or check whether a move is legal. Do not build or use a Go engine, run Monte Carlo, search over sequences of future moves, or write a program that chooses, ranks or recommends moves.

## How this session ends

Play until the game is over. The final result comes back from your last Go call, followed by a closing note. Before you end the session after a game, write down in your working directory whatever will help the next session play better. The session ends when you end your turn.

events.text:
G7 needs stabilizing, with the top-right corner F8-J9 plus H6 as the key eye space, and Black's E7 looming nearby. I'm weighing F8 versus H6 versus a hane at F7, but F7 is a direct contact move with limited liberties, so I'm also considering a base-building move like E8 instead.

Actually F8 blocks Black from sliding underneath, but there's also the side option at H6/H5 — these feel like miai, with the top (toward D8, contested near my C6) versus the lower-right side (toward G3/H3) being the real question of which is bigger. I'm also eyeing F6 as a splitting move that separates Black's E7 from G5 and strengthens G7 diagonally, accepting that Black can cut at F7 or G6 but I can answer whichever one they pick — though F6 alone doesn't give the group eye space yet.

Running the sequence further, F6 plus G7 ends up carving out eye space in the F8-J9 region worth around 10 points while also pressuring the weak G5 stone, so even if Black plays E6 solidly and cuts at G6 forcing me to connect at F7, my group should still live small in the top right while I hold the whole left side — rough count favors me around 42 versus Black's bottom-right. I'll commit to F6 over the more territorial H6.

events.text:
I lost game 180 to the 12k opponent. I played White and resigned at move 34, about 30 points behind, after my 9-stone top-right group died. My record as White against 12k is now 23 wins, 49 losses and 5 draws.

- **Opening:** C3 and C6 took the left side. When Black played E7 I went into the right half with G7, then followed with F6, a centre stone.
- **What went wrong:** Black cut at F7 and closed the group in with F8, H6 and J6, leaving only the small 3×3 top-right corner as eye space. Black's J8 stone inside the corner (move 29) and the E9 atari on my F9 stone (move 31) meant I could make the corner eye or the G9 eye, but not both. The group was left with 2 liberties (H8, J9) and only one possible eye.
- **Fix:** At move 8 I should have built the group's base along the right side (H5/H4) instead of playing F6 in the centre. Failing that, I should have secured the top edge (F9) and the corner shape (H8) before sealing moves like G8.

I added the move list, this analysis, a new lesson (−50) and next-game advice to `CLAUDE.md`. The lesson: a small corner with enemy stones two lines away on both sides can't make two eyes, so expand toward the open side first. The advice for next time: as White against 12k after E5 F3, follow the game-58 line and take the top (E7/D7) before Black does. As Black, play 14k with C3 + G3.
